name: Keshava Temple, Somanathapura
deity: Vishnu in three forms — Keshava, Janardhana and Venugopala (the central Keshava image is now lost)
summary: The last great Hoysala temple, finished in 1268 on the banks of the Kaveri — a perfectly unified three-shrined jewel, its sixteen carved ceilings and unbroken friezes representing the mature culmination of the entire Hoysala tradition.

sections.history: The Keshava temple was completed in 1268 CE by Somanatha Dandanayaka, a general and administrator under the Hoysala king Narasimha III, who founded the agrahara — the brahmin settlement — of Somanathapura and endowed this temple at its heart. Because it was built in a single sustained campaign late in the dynasty's life, it is the most complete and internally consistent of all Hoysala temples: nothing was left unfinished, and the design reads as one thought carried through. It came, however, near the end of Hoysala power, and after the disruptions of the fourteenth century the temple lost its central image and its worship lapsed. Today it is a protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India rather than a functioning shrine — yet its completeness makes it the clearest textbook of the style, and in 2023 UNESCO inscribed it with Belur and Halebidu as a Sacred Ensemble of the Hoysalas.
sections.architecture: Somanathapura is a trikuta — a three-celled temple — its three shrines opening off a common pillared hall so that the plan forms a compact, jewel-like whole set on the familiar star-shaped jagati within a colonnaded courtyard. It is the most integrated of Hoysala designs: the star-pointed walls carry continuous friezes of elephants, horsemen, epic narrative and rows of gods, all rendered in the deep soapstone carving the dynasty perfected, while the three towers rise in tiered miniature over the shrines. Inside, the glory is the ceilings — sixteen bays, each a different sunken design of lotuses and foliage worked to lace-like fineness. Several panels carry the signatures of their sculptors, among them the master Mallitamma, whose name recurs across the building. Where Belur charms and Halebidu overwhelms, Somanathapura resolves the tradition into balance.
sections.legends: The temple was dedicated to Vishnu as Keshava at the centre, flanked by Janardhana and Venugopala — Vishnu as Krishna the flute-player — so its walls dwell lovingly on the Krishna story alongside scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, a whole Vaishnava cosmology in stone. The central Keshava idol was lost in later centuries, and the empty sanctum is itself part of the temple's story, a reminder of the turbulence that ended the Hoysala age. What endures is the artists' presence: the signed panels make Somanathapura one of the rare medieval monuments where we can name the hands that made it, and later admirers have long treated the building as the signature achievement of the sculptors' guild.
sections.festivals: Somanathapura is a deconsecrated monument and no longer hosts daily worship or a temple festival calendar. Its rhythms today are those of a heritage site — quietest on weekday mornings, busier on weekends and holidays. Visitors seeking active Hoysala worship will find it at the living sister temples of Belur and Halebidu; here the experience is contemplative and architectural rather than ritual.
sections.experience: Because it is compact and complete, Somanathapura is the easiest Hoysala temple to take in whole. Walk the courtyard colonnade first for the framed view of the three towers, then circle the star-shaped platform to follow the friezes, and finally step inside to look up — the sixteen ceilings are the highlight, best seen when sunlight rakes across their carving. It sits on the Kaveri about 35 km from Mysuru, and pairs naturally with a Mysuru visit; unlike the living temples, its status as an ASI monument means the whole building, inside and out, is open to unhurried study.

visit.timings: Open daily, roughly 8:30 am to 5:30 pm, as an ASI-ticketed monument (there is a small entry fee). It is not a functioning temple, so there are no worship hours.
visit.dressCode: There is no ritual dress code, but modest, comfortable clothing is appropriate at a sacred heritage site; footwear is removed before stepping onto the temple platform.
visit.photography: Photography is freely permitted throughout, inside and out — one of the few Hoysala interiors where the celebrated ceilings can be photographed at leisure.
visit.gettingThere: Somanathapura is in Mysuru district on the Kaveri, about 35 km east of Mysuru and roughly 140 km from Bengaluru; Mysuru is the nearest railway and air hub.
